session: Session 1 - Why keep accounts: the three statements
bullets: Financial accounting: record transactions, classify them, then prepare statements giving a true and fair view. Management accounting is a separate (Semester 2) course.
Users: investors (profitability), banks and suppliers (ability to repay), customers (viability), government (taxes, GDP), employees.
Balance sheet at the closing date: assets (economic resources) = equity + liabilities (financial resources). Equity = assets − liabilities.
Income statement: income − expenses = net income for the fiscal year (profit or loss). Expenses and income are flows.
Statement of Cash Flows: operating + investing + financing = change in cash; plus opening cash = closing cash. Overdrafts sit in liabilities.
Every transaction keeps the equation balanced. Example: purchase 100 and resale 160 on credit gives net income +60 but no cash impact.
Profit and cash are two different things: net income is part of equity, cash is an asset.
Standards vary: PCG in France, IFRS for listed groups, local frameworks elsewhere. Closing date, closing by the board, approval by shareholders are three different dates.
examTip: Show the effect of each transaction on the balance sheet, net income and cash separately; never confuse profit with cash.

session: Session 2 - Exploring the accounting system and where the profit goes
bullets: Accounts are the most detailed level of recording (T-account: debit left, credit right). Nothing is ever erased in accounting.
Accounts on the left of the statements increase with debits, accounts on the right with credits. Balance = |Σ debits − Σ credits|.
A journal entry uses at least two accounts, e.g. credit sale: trade receivables and sales.
Income tax = taxable profit × rate. Example: income 680,000, expenses 300,000, accounting profit 380,000, tax 20% gives 80,000 and profit 300,000.
Tax for year N is an expense of N but paid in N+1, so it is a liability at closing.
Opening balances: the closing balance sheet of N is copied to open N+1; the income statement restarts at zero.
Allocation of profit (decided the following year) can only be retained earnings or dividends. Retained earnings cannot be used to pay expenses.
Example: profit 300,000, dividends 60,000, retained 240,000. Dividends are not an expense and appear in financing cash flows.
examTip: Remember tax is calculated on taxable profit, then net income = accounting profit − tax; dividends reduce equity, not net income.

session: Session 3 - The operating cycle and accrual accounting
bullets: Profit (operating, timing of amounts) is different from liquidity (cash on hand, timing of payments): a company can be profitable but short of cash.
Financial accounting uses accrual accounting, not cash-basis: record sales when delivered or service rendered, not when paid.
Classify purchases by use: fixed assets (more than one year), inventories (for resale or production), expenses (consumed in the year).
Credit purchase of an expense: expense and trade payables increase, no cash impact. Credit purchase of merchandise: inventories and trade payables increase, no expense yet.
Sale of goods records two things: revenue (with receivable or cash) and cost of sales (inventory drawdown). Sale 800 of goods costing 300 gives margin 500.
Services: only the sale is recorded.
Payroll: net salary = gross − employee contributions. Cost to company = gross + employer contributions. Example 250 + 75 = 325 expense.
Salary liabilities: wages payable 205 and social security payable 120 (75 + 45) until paid.
examTip: For every sale ask two questions: revenue and cost of sales; and always distinguish the income statement effect from the cash effect.

session: Session 5 - The investment cycle: fixed assets and depreciation
bullets: Fixed asset: held more than one year. Acquisition cost = purchase price less discounts + costs to make it ready (transport, installation, inspection). Training and maintenance are expenses.
Recognition: PP&E up and payable up; payment is an investing cash outflow (e.g. 24,000).
Depreciation (straight-line): gross amount × rate (100%/life) × pro rata temporis. Land and non-current financial assets are not depreciated.
Example: cost 24,000, life 4 years, from 1 April X1: X1 = 24,000 × 25% × 9/12 = 4,500; carrying amount 19,500; schedule spans 5 fiscal years.
Carrying amount = gross carrying amount − accumulated depreciation. Depreciation is an expense with no cash payment.
Disposal: stop depreciation at the sale date, remove gross cost and accumulated depreciation, gain or loss = proceeds − carrying amount.
Example: carrying amount 7,500, sold for 8,000 gives gain 500; proceeds go to investing cash flows. Proceeds below carrying amount is a loss.
Fixed asset roll-forward note: opening + increases − decreases = closing, for gross amount and for accumulated depreciation.
examTip: Compute months of use for the first and last years, and use carrying amount (not cost) to find the gain or loss on disposal.

session: Session 6 - The financing cycle: capital and loans
bullets: Two sources: shareholders (share capital, share premium, retained earnings) and borrowings (repayable with interest, a liability).
Shareholders: voting, dividends if distributed, limited liability, last paid in liquidation. Dividends are not an expense; interest is a finance cost and lowers tax.
Share capital = shares × par value (10,000 × 10 = 100,000). Share premium = new shares × (issue price − par value).
Example: 2,000 new shares at 15, par 10: cash +30,000, capital +20,000, premium +10,000, a financing inflow.
Book value per share = equity / shares (130,000 / 12,000 ≈ 10.83). Market price reflects expected future profits (216,000 at 18).
Loan receipt: cash and borrowings up, no income, financing inflow. Interest = opening principal × rate; only interest is an expense.
Three repayment types: balloon (interest only, then all principal), constant principal (50,000/5 = 10,000, falling interest), constant annuity (11,549 each year).
In year 1 of the 11,549 annuity: interest 2,500 (operating cash flow in the example), repayment 9,049 (financing).
examTip: Build the amortisation table: interest on the opening balance, then principal = installment − interest; only interest hits net income.

session: Session 7 - Year-end entries part 1: prudence principle (provisions and impairments)
bullets: Prudence: recognise probable losses and risks when they arise, not when they are paid. Gains are recognised only when realised.
Fixed asset impairment: recoverable amount = max(fair value less costs of disposal, value in use). Impairment loss if carrying amount exceeds it.
Example: carrying amount 18,350 against recoverable 52,000 means no loss. Mediasud: carrying 42,000 vs recoverable 33,000 gives loss 9,000.
Inventory: compare cost with net realisable value (selling price − selling costs), item by item. Boards: cost 8,000, NRV 7,000, impairment 1,000.
Expected margins on other items cannot offset a loss; each item is measured separately.
Receivable impairment: expected collection 4,000 × 70% = 2,800, so impairment 1,200. Impairment = required accumulated amount − previous amount.
Provision needs three conditions: present obligation from a past event, probable outflow, reliable estimate. Otherwise no entry or a contingent liability note.
Provision example: lawsuit 11,200 (not 25,000 claimed); next year paid 8,000, 3,200 reversed to income; warranty provision 3,000,000 × 2% × 50% = 30,000. No cash impact in year recognised.
examTip: Check the three provision conditions explicitly, and remember impairments and provisions hit profit but not cash at the time.

session: Session 8 - Year-end entries part 2: cut-off (prepaid, deferred, accrued)
bullets: Cut-off principle: the income statement of a year includes all expenses and income of that year, whatever the invoice date. Compare the invoice date with delivery or service date.
Accrued expense: service received before closing, invoice not received. Increase expenses and a liability (trade payables). Example: December electricity estimated at 500.
Accrued interest: 50,000 × 5% × 3/12 = 625 added to borrowings, no cash impact.
Accrued revenue: service done, invoice not issued. Increase revenue and trade receivables. Example: consulting 2,000.
Prepaid expense: invoice recorded but service after closing. Reduce expenses, asset (prepaid expenses). Example: 3,000 × 1/3 = 1,000.
Deferred revenue: income recorded for service after closing. Reduce revenue, liability (deferred revenue). Example: 12,000 × 3/12 = 3,000.
Prepaid expenses are assets and deferred revenue is a liability despite the names.
Adjustments never involve cash at closing: cash moves when invoices are paid or collected.
examTip: Work out the fraction of the period falling after year end, then decide which of the four adjustments applies and which side of the balance sheet it lands on.

session: Session 9 - The Statement of Cash Flows and linking the three statements
bullets: Cash receipts and payments change net cash. Net cash = cash and cash equivalents − bank overdrafts.
Expense is not a cash payment and income is not a cash receipt: depreciation is an expense with no cash; a bank loan is a receipt but not income.
Not in the statement: unsettled credit sales and purchases, provision expenses, impairment losses and reversals.

Operating: customers, suppliers, employees, taxes, interest paid (under current rules). Investing: purchases and disposals of fixed assets. Financing: share issues, dividends, borrowings and repayments.
Change in cash + opening cash = closing cash.
Link: the income statement explains net income; the Statement of Cash Flows explains the change in cash; balance sheet items link opening and closing.
Receivables roll: 13,000 opening + 84,000 sales − 72,000 collections = 12,000 closing.
Per transaction ask: cash impact? net income impact? the other balance sheet item? Checks: assets = equity + liabilities, profits match, closing cash matches.
examTip: Classify each cash flow into operating, investing or financing correctly and exclude non-cash items; if a check shows FALSE, the error is in the last transaction.
